Phylogenetic Isometric Log-Ratio Transform (PhILR)

Source: R/philr.r
philr.Rd

Silverman et al.'s PhILR coordinates: an isometric log-ratio transform whose balances follow a phylogeny. Each internal node of the tree gives one coordinate, the log ratio of its two child clades' (weighted) geometric means, so every coordinate has an evolutionary meaning: "this clade against its sister clade".

Usage

philr(
  counts,
  tree = NULL,
  margin = 1L,
  pseudocount = NULL,
  part_weights = "uniform",
  ilr_weights = "uniform",
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

Arguments

counts

A numeric matrix of counts or proportions (samples \(\times\) features, see margin), or an object of one of the types in Input Types. Its features must have names, matched to the tips of tree. Counts, proportions and the output of replace_zeros() are all accepted, with one caveat: the 'gm.counts' part weights assume counts.

tree

A phylo object whose tips include every feature of counts, or NULL to use the tree inside counts (a phyloseq, rbiom or TreeSummarizedExperiment object, or attr(counts, 'tree')). See The tree.

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

pseudocount

Added to every value before taking logs. NULL (the default) adds nothing when counts has no zeros, and otherwise uses half the smallest non-zero value, with a warning. See Pseudocount.

part_weights

The weights \(p_j\) of the features (philr's part.weights), which set the reference measure of the simplex. One of

  • 'uniform' (the default): all 1, the usual ilr;

  • 'gm.counts': each feature's geometric mean over the samples (of counts + pseudocount);

  • 'enorm': the Euclidean norm of each feature's values over the samples, after closing them to sum to 1 (so that a feature found in only a few samples gets a weight near 1, and one spread evenly over \(n\) samples gets \(1/\sqrt{n}\));

  • 'anorm': the Aitchison norm of each feature's values over the samples, \(\sqrt{\sum_k (\log x_{kj} - \overline{\log x_j})^2}\);

  • 'enorm.x.gm.counts' and 'anorm.x.gm.counts': products of the two;

  • a vector of positive numbers, one per feature, named by feature (or in the order of the features of counts).

Names may also be written with underscores ('gm_counts'). The weights computed from counts depend on every sample, so one sample's coordinates depend on the others.

ilr_weights

The weights \(f_i\) of the coordinates (philr's ilr.weights), which scale each balance. One of

  • 'uniform' (the default): all 1;

  • 'blw': the sum of the node's two child branch lengths;

  • 'blw.sqrt': its square root;

  • 'mean.descendants': the sum of the two child branch lengths plus, for each child, its mean distance to its tips;

  • a vector of non-negative numbers, one per coordinate, named by coordinate (or in the order of the coordinates).

For the branch-length weights, zero-length branches to tips first get the smallest positive branch length of the tree, as in philr. They need tree to have branch lengths.

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), will use all logical CPU cores.

Value

A dense numeric matrix of the \(D - 1\) coordinates, one per internal node of the tree, in the orientation of counts: samples \(\times\) coordinates for margin = 1, coordinates \(\times\) samples for margin = 2. Sample names are kept. Coordinates are named by the tree's node labels when every node has a distinct one (nodes added to resolve a polytomy at node "X" get "X.1", "X.2", ...), and otherwise n1, n2, ..., in column order. Attributes:

  • method: 'philr'.

  • part_weights: the part weights used, named by feature, in the order of the features of counts.

  • ilr_weights: the ILR weights used, named by coordinate.

  • tree: the tree used, as a phylo object (see The tree). Its internal nodes are numbered and labelled in column order (node \(D + k\) is coordinate \(k\)), and for each node, its first child in tree$edge is the numerator ("+") clade.

  • pseudocount: the pseudocount used (0 for none).

These are what philr's return.all = TRUE gives as p, ilr.weights and (through the tree) sbp. Its contrast matrix V is not kept: it has \(D (D - 1)\) entries.

Details

For a sample \(x\) (with the pseudocount added) and part weights \(p\), write \(y_j = x_j / p_j\). At an internal node with clades \(A\) (its first child, the numerator) and \(B\) (its second), let \(n_A = \sum_{j \in A} p_j\) and \(\log g_A = \sum_{j \in A} p_j \log y_j / n_A\) (and likewise for \(B\)). The node's coordinate is $$f \sqrt{\frac{n_A n_B}{n_A + n_B}}\,\left(\log g_A - \log g_B\right),$$ with \(f\) its ILR weight (Silverman et al. 2017, Methods). It is computed in \(O(D)\) per sample, by summing over each clade from the tips up, without forming the \(D \times (D - 1)\) basis.

With uniform weights the coordinates are an ordinary ilr: they equal ilr(counts, basis = sbp) for the tree's sequential binary partition, and euclidean(philr(x, tree)) is aitchison(x) (with the same pseudocount), as for any orthonormal basis. It is the weights that make distances phylogenetic: philr_distance() uses the paper's.

The coordinates feed straight into pca(), rda(), lda(), envfit() and euclidean(), which take negative values with norm = 'none'.

philr(x, tree, pseudocount = c, part_weights = pw, ilr_weights = iw) equals philr 1.28.0's philr(x, tree, part.weights = pw, ilr.weights = iw, pseudocount = c) to rounding, for every weighting and for a binary tree whose tips are the features of x.

The tree

PhILR needs a rooted binary tree whose tips are the features. tree is made one in three steps (the result is the tree attribute):

  1. Tips that aren't features of counts are dropped, and so are the internal nodes left without any. Every feature must be a tip.

  2. Nodes left with one child are removed, their branch length added to their child's (a root with one child is dropped), as ape::drop.tip() does.

  3. Polytomies are resolved, with a warning: a node with children \(c_1, \dots, c_k\), \(k > 2\), keeps \(c_1\) and gets a new child node, joined by a zero-length branch, that holds \(c_2, \dots, c_k\) (and so on), as ape::multi2di(random = FALSE) does. An unrooted tree (three children at the root) is resolved the same way. Results then depend on the order of the children: to choose the resolution, resolve the tree first.

Coordinates are in the order of the internal nodes' numbers in tree (the root first), or, when a step changed the tree, in preorder of the new tree (which is also the order of ape::multi2di()'s and ape::drop.tip()'s numbering). Branch lengths are needed only for the branch-length ILR weights; they must be non-negative. A root edge is ignored.

Same names in other packages: philr::philr() computes the same transform, with the same orientation and order. Whichever package was attached last masks the other's philr(); write ecodive::philr() to be sure.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

Pseudocount

Logs of zero are undefined, so zeros need replacing first. The pseudocount is added to every value (not only to zeros), as in normalize(norm = 'clr'). With pseudocount = NULL (the default), no pseudocount is used when counts has no zeros; otherwise half the smallest non-zero value is, with a warning. To avoid a pseudocount, replace the zeros first with replace_zeros(): its result has none.

The choice of pseudocount is not neutral: it can distort the results, especially for sparse tables. See aitchison() for references.

References

Silverman, J. D., Washburne, A. D., Mukherjee, S., & David, L. A. (2017). A phylogenetic transform enhances analysis of compositional microbiota data. eLife, 6, e21887. doi:10.7554/eLife.21887

Egozcue, J. J., & Pawlowsky-Glahn, V. (2016). Changing the reference measure in the simplex and its weighting effects. Austrian Journal of Statistics, 45(4), 25–44. doi:10.17713/ajs.v45i4.126

See also

philr_distance(), ilr(), aitchison()

Examples

    x <- philr(ex_counts, tree = ex_tree, pseudocount = 1)
    dim(x)
#> [1] 4 5
    x[1:3, 1:4]
#>               n1       n2        n3        n4
#> Saliva  1.965104 2.899056  2.200302  3.601825
#> Gums    1.186504 2.027911  3.338542  4.231282
#> Nose   -4.604698 0.000000 -1.569240 -1.649373

    # With uniform weights, distances are Aitchison distances
    all.equal(
      as.vector(euclidean(x)),
      as.vector(aitchison(ex_counts, pseudocount = 1)) )
#> [1] TRUE

    # The paper's weights
    x <- philr(
      ex_counts, tree = ex_tree, pseudocount = 1,
      part_weights = 'enorm.x.gm.counts', ilr_weights = 'blw.sqrt' )
    head(attr(x, 'ilr_weights'))
#>        n1        n2        n3        n4        n5 
#>  3.605551 10.583005  4.898979  5.385165  6.082763
